text: Chapter One covered how any LLM works under the hood. Chapter Two is about the actual landscape — who makes these models, and what they're each called right now. Checked directly against every provider's own documentation, because this list moves fast.

Five names to know. Anthropic's Claude: Haiku, Sonnet, Opus, and Fable tiers, Fable currently the flagship. OpenAI's GPT: the six-point-x Astra family at the top, with Sol and Luna nearby. Google's Gemini: the three-point-eight Flash generation, plus a Pro Preview tier. xAI's Grok: four-point-seven, five hundred thousand tokens of context. And Meta's Llama: four, open-weighted instead of API-only — Lesson 9 explains exactly what that distinction means.

Three pieces, every name. The family — Claude, GPT, Gemini — identifies the lineage. The generation number marks a major version bump. And the tier name — Haiku, Sonnet, Opus, Fable, or Flash, Pro — marks where it sits on the speed-versus-capability trade-off from last lesson. Parse it that way, and a release you've never seen still tells you roughly what it's for.

The same four-ish-tier pattern repeats at every provider — cheap and fast, balanced, flagship — even though the names differ completely. What actually differs more is positioning: Anthropic leans into coding and agentic work, OpenAI has the broadest consumer ecosystem, Google leans on its own cloud and multimodal strengths, xAI positions itself as lean and cost-conscious.

Five families, four-ish tiers each, and a naming pattern that holds up across all of them. Next lesson: the other major split in this landscape — open-weight models you can download, versus closed models you can only call through an API.
